title: Internet, Browsers & E-mail
summary: Internet history and structure, browsers vs search engines, URL/DNS, e-mail mechanics (To/CC/BCC, SMTP/POP3/IMAP) and India's e-banking rails (UPI, NEFT, RTGS). Full forms and the browser-vs-engine trap are asked every year.

subtopics.title: Internet, WWW, URL and DNS
subtopics.concept:
The **Internet** is a global 'network of networks' that grew out of **ARPANET** (1969, US DoD project; first nodes UCLA and Stanford). The **TCP/IP** protocol suite became its standard on 1 January 1983. The **World Wide Web** is one service running on the Internet - the system of interlinked web pages invented by **Tim Berners-Lee in 1989 at CERN** (with the first browser/editor, WorldWideWeb). Other services: e-mail, FTP, VoIP, streaming.

An **ISP** (Internet Service Provider - Jio, Airtel, BSNL) sells you connectivity and assigns an **IP address**. The **DNS (Domain Name System)** is the Internet's phonebook: it converts a name like www.ssc.gov.in into its numeric IP address (this translation is its exam definition).

**URL (Uniform Resource Locator)** parts: `https://www.ssc.gov.in:443/exams/index.html` = protocol + subdomain + domain + top-level domain (TLD .in) + port + path + file. Common TLDs: .com (commercial), .org (organisation), .edu (education), .gov (government), .in (India). **Bandwidth** = data-carrying capacity (bps/Kbps/Mbps); broadband = always-on high-speed access (fibre, DSL, 4G/5G).

tricks.title: Internet vs WWW
tricks.body: The **Internet = hardware network** (cables, routers, servers); the **WWW = content service** (hyperlinked pages) riding on it. Invented later (1989) by ONE man - Berners-Lee; the Internet is older (1969 ARPANET).

example.q: Who invented the World Wide Web?
example.solution: Tim Berners-Lee (CERN, 1989).

tricks.title: DNS = phonebook
tricks.body: DNS translates names to numbers - never 'assigns IPs' (that is DHCP) and never 'sends mail' (that is SMTP). Any question phrased 'converts domain names into IP addresses' = DNS.

example.q: What does DNS do?
example.solution: Resolves domain names into IP addresses.

mistakes: Treating WWW and the Internet as the same thing.
Saying DNS assigns IP addresses - DHCP assigns; DNS resolves names to IPs.
Dating the Internet to 1989 - that is the WWW; ARPANET was 1969.
subtopics.notes:
### Internet and WWW — related but not the same
The **Internet** is a worldwide **network of networks**: millions of computers and phones connected so they can exchange data. It grew out of **ARPANET**, a 1969 project of the US Defence Department (its first two nodes were UCLA and Stanford). The **World Wide Web (WWW)** is a **service that runs on the Internet** — the collection of hyperlinked pages read through a browser. It was invented by **Tim Berners-Lee in 1989** at CERN. E-mail and file transfer are other services on the same Internet. So: Internet = the road system, WWW = one kind of traffic on it.

### URL — the address of a page
A **URL (Uniform Resource Locator)** names every page. Read it in parts:

`https://www.example.in/Results/2026.html`
- **https://** — the protocol (rules for the conversation). HTTPS is the **secure** version (encrypted); plain HTTP is not.
- **www.example.in** — the **domain name** of the server (www = world wide web host prefix, .in = India country code; .com, .org, .gov, .edu are others).
- **/Results/2026.html** — the **path** to the exact page or file on that server.

The **DNS (Domain Name System)** translates the typed name into the server's **IP address** — the numeric identity (like 142.250.183.14) that machines actually use. DNS is the **phonebook of the Internet**: you ask for a name, it returns the number.

### Who does what on the net
| Player | Job |
|---|---|
| **ISP** (Internet Service Provider) | sells you the connection (Jio, Airtel, BSNL) |
| **DNS server** | name to IP address translation |
| **DHCP server** | **assigns** an IP address to your device |
| **Web server** | stores pages and serves them to browsers |

Classic trap: **DNS resolves names; DHCP assigns addresses.**

### Small facts that recur
- **IP address** — a device's numeric address; IPv4 has four blocks of 0-255.
- **TCP/IP** is the standard protocol suite of the Internet (ARPANET adopted it in 1983).
- **Bandwidth** is the data-carrying capacity of a link; **latency** is the delay.
- **VoIP** (Voice over Internet Protocol) carries phone calls over the Internet.
- A **web portal** is a site that gathers many services on one page; a **website** is a set of related web pages under one domain.

### How the pieces cooperate (one page load)
1. You type a **URL** in the browser.
2. **DNS** turns the domain into the server's IP address.
3. Your request travels over TCP/IP to the **web server**, which sends the page back.
4. The browser renders the HTML and displays the page — all in about a second.
Every exam question on DNS, URL or ISP is one stop on this journey, so picture it as a single delivery trip: name translated (DNS), address found (IP), parcel carried (TCP/IP), delivered by the shop (web server).

### Quick revision
- Internet = network of networks (from ARPANET, 1969); WWW = hyperlinked pages (Berners-Lee, 1989).
- URL = protocol + domain + path; https is the secure protocol.
- **DNS: name to IP; DHCP: gives IP; ISP: sells the connection.**
- TCP/IP = the Internet's protocol suite; VoIP = calls over the Internet.

patterns.name: Internet vs WWW and ARPANET history
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Internet is', 'WWW was invented by', 'the year of ARPANET' or a statement question mixing the Internet with the Web.
patterns.logic:
1. Internet = the global network of networks, born from **ARPANET (1969)**.
2. WWW = the hyperlinked-page service, invented by **Tim Berners-Lee, 1989, CERN**.
3. The Web is a service ON the Internet (with e-mail, FTP); the two words are not interchangeable.

example.q: The World Wide Web was invented in 1989 by:
example.solution: **Tim Berners-Lee** at CERN — the Internet itself is older, growing from ARPANET of 1969.

patterns.name: URL anatomy
patterns.howToSpot: A URL is given and a part is asked: the protocol, the domain, the country code, the path — or the full form of URL.
patterns.logic:
1. Split at the slashes: https:// + domain + path.
2. The part before the first single slash after the address is the protocol; the name before the first single slash is the domain; what follows is the path.
3. Ending codes: .com commercial, .org organisation, .gov government, .edu education, .in India.

example.q: In https://www.mysite.in/exams/ssc.html, the domain name is:
example.solution: **www.mysite.in** — https is the protocol, /exams/ssc.html is the path to the page.

patterns.name: DNS, DHCP and ISP roles
patterns.howToSpot: 'DNS converts ___ to ___', 'which server assigns IP addresses', 'who provides the Internet connection' — role-matching of the three servers.
patterns.logic:
1. **DNS = Domain Name System**: domain name to IP address (the phonebook).
2. **DHCP = Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol**: ASSIGNS IP addresses to devices.
3. **ISP** sells the connection. The swap of DNS and DHCP jobs is the planted error.

example.q: The server that converts a website name into its IP address is the:
example.solution: **DNS server** — assigning addresses is DHCP's job; resolving names is DNS's.

patterns.name: Internet full forms and firsts
patterns.howToSpot: 'Full form of HTTP/HTML/URL/ISP/VoIP' or wrongly matched pairs where one word of the expansion is changed.
patterns.logic:
1. HTTP = HyperText Transfer Protocol; HTML = HyperText Markup Language; URL = Uniform Resource Locator; ISP = Internet Service Provider; VoIP = Voice over Internet Protocol; WWW = World Wide Web.
2. Check word by word — 'Hyper Transfer Text Protocol' style traps are common.
3. HTML is a MARKUP language, not a programming language.

example.q: The full form of HTML is:
example.solution: **HyperText Markup Language** — the language in which web pages are written; it is a markup language, not a programming language.

subtopics.title: Browsers, search engines, downloading and uploading
subtopics.concept:
A **browser** is the client software that fetches and displays web pages: Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Firefox, Safari, Opera. A **search engine** is a website that indexes the web and finds pages: Google, Bing, Yahoo, DuckDuckGo. (Google is NOT a browser; Chrome is NOT a search engine - the most repeated trap.)

A **webpage** is one document (HTML); a **website** is a collection of related pages; the **home page** is a site's opening page; a **portal** bundles services (news, mail, shopping). Pages are written in **HTML** (HyperText Markup Language) and linked by **hyperlinks**.

**Downloading** = copying files FROM a server to your device; **uploading** = sending files FROM your device TO a server (e.g. attaching to e-mail, posting videos). **Cookies** are small text files a site stores in your browser (sessions, preferences, tracking); the **cache** keeps copies of pages/images for faster reloads.

**Search tips:** quotes "exact phrase", minus -exclude, site:ssc.gov.in restricts to a site, OR widens. **Browser shortcuts:** Ctrl+T new tab, Ctrl+W close tab, Ctrl+Shift+T reopen closed tab, Ctrl+N window, Ctrl+Shift+N incognito/private, Ctrl+D bookmark, Ctrl+H history, Ctrl+J downloads, F5 refresh, Ctrl+F5 hard refresh, Ctrl+F find in page, Ctrl+L/Alt+D address bar, Ctrl+Enter adds www...com, Ctrl+plus/minus/0 zoom, F11 full screen, Ctrl+S save page, Ctrl+U view source, Ctrl+P print.

tricks.title: Browser vs engine
tricks.body: **Browser = the car; search engine = the GPS you ask inside it.** Chrome/Edge/Firefox/Safari/Opera = cars. Google/Bing/Yahoo/DuckDuckGo = GPS. If it is a program you install, browser; if it is a website you visit, engine.

example.q: Which of these is a web browser - Google, Chrome, Yahoo, Bing?
example.solution: Chrome (the rest are search engines).

tricks.title: Ctrl-letter browser map
tricks.body: **T**ab new, **W**ipe (close) tab, **D**rop a bookmark, **H**istory, **J**unk... no - **J**etisoned files (Downloads), **N**ormal window, **N+Shift** No-trace (incognito). F5 = freshen.

example.q: Shortcut to reopen a closed tab?
example.solution: Ctrl+Shift+T.

tricks.title: Up vs Down
tricks.body: **Upload = YOU send up** (to the server); **Download = server sends down** to you. The direction is always relative to YOUR machine.

example.q: Saving an e-mail attachment to your PC is?
example.solution: Downloading.

mistakes: Calling Google a browser or Chrome a search engine.

Confusing Ctrl+H (history) with Ctrl+J (downloads) - H comes before J alphabetically: History before Downloads? No: History=H, Downloads=J is pure memory; the mnemonic is 'H = havens visited (history)'.
Thinking cookies are viruses - cookies are passive text files (privacy issue, not malware).
subtopics.notes:
### Browser vs search engine — separate jobs
A **browser** is the **program on your device** that fetches and displays web pages: **Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Firefox, Safari, Opera** (Internet Explorer is retired). A **search engine** is a **website** that indexes the web and finds pages for your words: **Google, Bing, Yahoo, DuckDuckGo**. Google is a search engine; Chrome is a browser; Chrome's address bar can USE Google. Exams love the swap: "Google is a browser — true or false?" False.

### The browser's everyday tools
| Tool | What it keeps |
|---|---|
| **History** | every page you visited |
| **Bookmarks/Favourites** | pages you saved for quick return |
| **Cache** | copies of pages and pictures, so revisits load faster |
| **Cookies** | small text files a site stores on you — logins, preferences, tracking |

Cookies are **not viruses** — they are passive text files; the worry is privacy, not infection. **Incognito / private mode** opens a window that forgets history and cookies when closed — useful on shared computers. It does **not** make you anonymous to the websites or the ISP.

### Keyboard shortcuts of the browser
| Key | Job |
|---|---|
| **Ctrl+T** | new **T**ab |
| **Ctrl+N** | new window |
| **Ctrl+Shift+N** | new **incognito** window (Chrome) |
| **Ctrl+H** | **H**istory panel |
| **Ctrl+J** | **J**ust-downloaded files (downloads list) |
| **Ctrl+D** | **D**rop a bookmark |
| **Ctrl+F** | **F**ind text on the page |
| **F5 / Ctrl+R** | refresh the page |

H before J alphabetically: **History, then downloads** — a common one-mark trap.

### Downloading and uploading
- **Download** = a file travels from a server **to your device** (songs, PDFs, apps). The browser's downloads list (Ctrl+J) tracks them; the Downloads folder stores them.
- **Upload** = a file travels from **your device to a server** (attaching a form, posting a video).
- **Streaming** = watching or listening as the data arrives, without saving the whole file first.

### Using a search engine well
Type specific **keywords**, not full sentences; put quotes around words that must appear together ("solar mission"); a minus sign removes a word. Results mix ads, links, images and videos — the engine ranks pages by relevance, it does not check truth.

### Quick revision
- Chrome/Edge/Firefox/Safari = browsers; Google/Bing/DuckDuckGo = search engines.
- History (Ctrl+H), downloads (Ctrl+J), bookmark (Ctrl+D), new tab (Ctrl+T), incognito Ctrl+Shift+N.
- Cache = speed copies; cookies = site-stored text files (privacy, not viruses).
- Download = server to you; upload = you to server; streaming = play as it arrives.

patterns.name: Browser vs search engine
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which one is a browser/search engine?' or odd-one-out among Chrome, Firefox, Google, Safari — with Google planted among browsers.
patterns.logic:
1. Browsers (programs): Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari, Opera.
2. Search engines (websites): Google, Bing, Yahoo, DuckDuckGo.
3. The classic trap: Google listed among browsers or Chrome listed among search engines.

example.q: Which of the following is a WEB BROWSER?
example.solution: **Chrome** (like Edge, Firefox, Safari) — Google and Bing are search engines, programs that live inside browsers.

patterns.name: Browser shortcut recall
patterns.howToSpot: 'Shortcut to open a new tab / history / downloads / bookmark' — with Ctrl+H and Ctrl+J swapped in the options.
patterns.logic:
1. Ctrl+T new Tab, Ctrl+N new window, Ctrl+Shift+N incognito, **Ctrl+H History**, **Ctrl+J downloads**, Ctrl+D bookmark, Ctrl+F find on page, F5 refresh.
2. H before J: History first, downloads (J) second.
3. Ctrl+D is bookmark in browsers but fill-down in Excel — context decides.

example.q: The keyboard shortcut that opens the downloads list in Chrome is:
example.solution: **Ctrl+J** — Ctrl+H opens History instead.

patterns.name: Download, upload, cache and cookies
patterns.howToSpot: 'Downloading means', 'what does the browser cache store', 'cookies are ___' — direction or definition matching.
patterns.logic:
1. **Download** = server to your device; **upload** = your device to server; streaming = play while it arrives.
2. Cache = copies kept for faster revisits; history = list of visits.
3. **Cookies = small text files** a site saves (login, preferences, tracking) — passive files, not viruses.

example.q: Receiving a file from a web server to your computer is called:
example.solution: **Downloading** — sending one the other way is uploading.

patterns.name: Incognito and privacy features
patterns.howToSpot: 'Incognito mode ___', 'private browsing saves ___' — what is forgotten, what is NOT hidden.
patterns.logic:
1. Incognito/private windows **forget history and cookies after closing** — good for shared computers.
2. They do NOT hide you from websites, the office network or the ISP, and bookmarks you make stay.
3. Cookies cleared = stored logins lost in that window.

example.q: Which statement about Chrome's Incognito mode is TRUE?
example.solution: **Browsing history and cookies of that window are deleted when it closes** — but your ISP and the websites still see the visit.

subtopics.title: E-mail: structure, To/CC/BCC and protocols
subtopics.concept:
**E-mail** (electronic mail) exchanges messages between accounts on mail servers. An address = `username@domain` - the **@** separates user from domain (ray.kiran@gmail.com).

**Fields:** **To** - primary recipients; **CC (Carbon Copy)** - secondary recipients visible to all; **BCC (Blind Carbon Copy)** - hidden recipients: the To/CC people cannot see who was BCC'd (use BCC for mass mails to protect privacy). Others: Subject, body, **attachment** (paperclip; files sent along, size-limited), signature, priority.

**Folders/actions:** Compose, Send, Reply (to sender), Reply All (sender + everyone on To/CC), Forward (pass on), Inbox (received), Outbox (pending), Sent, Drafts (unfinished), Spam/Junk (filtered mail), Trash/Bin. **MIME** (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) is the standard that lets e-mail carry attachments, images and non-English text.

**Protocols:** **SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, port 25)** - SENDS mail between clients and servers. **POP3 (Post Office Protocol v3, port 110)** - downloads mail to one device, usually removing it from the server. **IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol, port 143)** - mail stays on the server and **syncs across many devices**. Webmail (Gmail in a browser) vs mail clients (Outlook, Thunderbird). Filters/labels sort automatically; autoresponders reply when you are away.

tricks.title: CC vs BCC
tricks.body: **CC = Carbon Copy - Everyone sees. BCC = Blind - eyes covered**, so To/CC recipients cannot see the blind list. 'Who was secretly copied?' - nobody but the sender knows.

example.q: A receiver of the mail can see the addresses in which field(s)?
example.solution: To and CC - never BCC.

tricks.title: SMTP Sends, POP Picks, IMAP In-sync
tricks.body: **S**MTP = **S**end (outgoing). **P**OP3 = **P**ick up on one device (downloads, server emptied). **IMAP = In All devices** (server copy stays, everything syncs).

example.q: Which protocol lets you read the same mail on phone and laptop?
example.solution: IMAP.

tricks.title: @ = at
tricks.body: In ray@gmail.com the @ separates 'who' from 'where' - user at domain. Options without @, or with a space/comma, are dead giveaways.

example.q: Which character separates the username from the domain in e-mail?
example.solution: @ (at the rate).

mistakes: Saying CC recipients are hidden - that is BCC; CC is fully visible.
Making SMTP the receiving protocol - SMTP only sends; POP3/IMAP receive.
Using Reply All when a mass mail was BCC'd - your reply reaches the sender, not the hidden list (and Reply-All storms are bad netiquette).
subtopics.notes:
### What e-mail is
**E-mail (electronic mail)** sends messages between accounts stored on **mail servers**. An address has two parts joined by **@** ("at"): `rani.sharma@gmail.com` — **username @ domain**. The domain here belongs to Gmail (Google's mail service); Outlook and Yahoo Mail are others. @ is the separator — a favourite full-form/identification question.

### The fields of a compose window
| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **To** | the main receivers |
| **CC** (Carbon Copy) | extra receivers — **everyone can see** all To and CC addresses |
| **BCC** (Blind Carbon Copy) | hidden receivers — **To and CC people cannot see** the BCC list; each BCC receiver also can't see the others |
| **Subject** | one-line summary of the mail |
| **Attachment** | files clipped to the mail (paperclip icon) |
| **Signature** | sender's fixed sign-off block |

**The CC/BCC rule:** CC is a visible copy; BCC is a blind copy. When a mail was sent with addresses in BCC, **Reply All reaches only the sender** — the hidden list stays hidden.

### The three protocols
| Protocol | Direction | How it works |
|---|---|---|
| **SMTP** (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) | **sending** (and passing between servers) | pushes your mail out |
| **POP3** (Post Office Protocol v3) | **receiving** | downloads mail to ONE device, usually deleting it from the server |
| **IMAP** (Internet Message Access Protocol) | **receiving** | mail **stays on the server**, synced across all your devices |

Memory hook: **SMTP Sends, POP Picks (down), IMAP In-sync.** If the question says "protocol used to SEND e-mail" — SMTP, every time.

### Everyday mail actions
- **Reply** answers only the sender; **Reply All** answers the sender and everyone in To/CC; **Forward** sends a received mail to new people.
- **Spam** = junk or unsolicited mail; the filter parks it in the Spam folder — never click its links.
- **Draft** = a mail written but not sent; it waits until you finish it.
- **Cc etiquette**: use CC to keep someone informed; use BCC for bulk mails so receivers' addresses stay private.

### The journey of one e-mail
1. Rani writes a mail and presses Send. Her mail server uses **SMTP** to push it across the Internet to the server named after the **@domain**.
2. The receiver's server holds the mail in her mailbox.
3. When the receiver opens her app, **IMAP** (or POP3) fetches or syncs it to her device.
So one mail may touch three protocols: SMTP out, IMAP in, and the two servers talking to each other by SMTP. Exams compress this story into one line — "SMTP is used to send" — but the full journey is worth one drawing in your rough notes.

### Quick revision
- Address = username @ domain; @ separates the two.
- **CC visible to all; BCC hidden** from To and CC receivers.
- **SMTP sends; POP3 downloads to one device; IMAP syncs everywhere.**
- Reply = sender; Reply All = everyone in To/CC; Forward = new receivers.
- Spam = junk mail; Draft = unsent mail.

patterns.name: CC/BCC visibility scenario
patterns.howToSpot: A mail-sending scenario asks who can see whom: 'addresses in BCC are visible to ___', or the field to use so receivers don't see each other.
patterns.logic:
1. **CC receivers are visible to everyone** (To and CC).
2. **BCC receivers are hidden** — To/CC people never see them; BCC people see To/CC but not each other.
3. Bulk mails to strangers go in BCC to protect addresses.

example.q: Ravi sends a mail to 200 customers with all addresses in BCC. If a customer presses Reply All, the reply goes to:
example.solution: **Only the sender** — the BCC list is hidden and other receivers are not disclosed.

patterns.name: Protocol direction: SMTP vs POP3 vs IMAP
patterns.howToSpot: 'Protocol used to SEND e-mail', 'which protocol downloads mail to one device', 'which protocol keeps mail synced on the server' — direction matching.
patterns.logic:
1. **SMTP = sending** (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol).
2. **POP3 = receiving, downloads to one device** (usually removes from server).
3. **IMAP = receiving, stays on server, syncs everywhere**.
4. Reversed pairs (SMTP as receiver, POP as sender) are the standard traps.

example.q: Which protocol is used to SEND an e-mail from the client to the mail server?
example.solution: **SMTP** — Simple Mail Transfer Protocol. POP3 and IMAP only fetch incoming mail.

patterns.name: E-mail address and fields anatomy
patterns.howToSpot: 'In rani@gmail.com, the part before @ is', 'what separates user and domain', or identification of Subject/Attachment/Signature fields.
patterns.logic:
1. Address = **username @ domain**; @ is the separator ('at').
2. Subject = one-line summary; attachment = clipped file (paperclip); signature = fixed sign-off.
3. The domain after @ names the mail service (gmail.com).

example.q: In the address kiran.verma@yahoo.in, the username is:
example.solution: **kiran.verma** — the @ separates the username from the domain (yahoo.in).

patterns.name: Reply, Reply All, Forward, Spam, Draft
patterns.howToSpot: A scenario on which action answers whom, or the meaning of spam / draft / forwarding.
patterns.logic:
1. **Reply** = only to the sender; **Reply All** = sender plus everyone in To/CC; **Forward** = passes the mail to new receivers.
2. **Spam** = junk mail, parked in the Spam folder by the filter.
3. **Draft** = written but not sent yet.

example.q: Swati received a circular sent to her whole class. She wants only the teacher to read her answer. She should use —
example.solution: **Reply** (to the sender) — Reply All would reach every classmate who was on To/CC.

subtopics.title: e-Banking and digital payments
subtopics.concept:
**e-Banking/net banking** = banking through the bank's secured website/app; **mobile banking** via apps; **ATM** (Automated Teller Machine) for cash, balance, mini-statement, PIN change.

**Payment systems (NPCI - National Payments Corporation of India, 2008 - runs most retail rails):**

| System | Nature | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| NEFT | National Electronic Funds Transfer | Batch/half-hourly settlement; no minimum; available 24x7 since Dec 2019 |
| RTGS | Real Time Gross Settlement | **Minimum Rs. 2 lakh**; settles individually, real time; 24x7 since Dec 2020 |
| IMPS | Immediate Payment Service | Instant 24x7 transfers via mobile/MMID; no RTGS-style minimum |
| UPI | Unified Payments Interface (2016) | Instant app-to-app transfer using a VPA (name@bank); 24x7; BHIM app; QR payments |

**Security tokens:** **IFSC** (Indian Financial System Code) - 11 characters identifying the bank branch (e.g. SBIN0001234); **MICR** 9-digit cheque code; **OTP** (One Time Password) and **2FA** (two-factor authentication: something you know + something you receive/are). Safety rules: banks NEVER ask for PIN/OTP/password; check https + padlock before paying; avoid public Wi-Fi for transactions; unknown links = phishing (see cyber-security topic).

tricks.title: NEFT vs RTGS
tricks.body: **RTGS = Really To Go, in batches of one, 2 lakh+** (real-time, gross = one-by-one, big amounts). **NEFT = Nice Easy Batches** (settlement in half-hourly batches, any amount).

example.q: Minimum amount for RTGS?
example.solution: Rs. 2 lakh.

tricks.title: IFSC 11
tricks.body: IFSC = **11 characters** (4 bank code + 0 + 6 branch code), used on NEFT/RTGS/UPI branch routing. MICR is the 9-digit cheque strip.

example.q: How many characters does an IFSC code have?

tricks.title: 2FA two keys
tricks.body: Two-factor = password (know) + OTP/biometric (have/are). One stolen password is not enough - that is the whole point.

example.q: Entering a password followed by an SMS OTP is an example of?
example.solution: Two-factor authentication.

mistakes: Giving NEFT the 2-lakh minimum - RTGS has it; NEFT has no minimum.
Saying IMPS is only for banks abroad - IMPS is an Indian instant retail rail.
Sharing OTPs on calls 'from the bank' - real banks never ask; that is vishing.
subtopics.notes:
### Banking from a distance
**e-Banking (net banking)** = banking through the bank's secured **website**; **mobile banking** = the same through an **app**. The **ATM (Automated Teller Machine)** works round the clock for cash withdrawal, balance enquiry, mini statement and PIN change. All of them sit on the same idea: instructions travel over secure networks instead of paper slips at a counter.

### The money-transfer rails of India
| Rail | Full form | Style |
|---|---|---|
| **NEFT** | National Electronic Funds Transfer | moves in **batches** (half-hourly slots); **no minimum**; 24x7 since 2019 |
| **RTGS** | Real Time Gross Settlement | **real-time, transaction by transaction**; **minimum 2,00,000 rupees** |
| **IMPS** | Immediate Payment Service | **instant**, runs inside mobile/internet banking, 24x7 |
| **UPI** | Unified Payments Interface | instant app-to-app transfer by **UPI ID or QR** (PhonePe, GPay, Paytm); built by **NPCI** (National Payments Corporation of India) |

RTGS's rule is asked again and again: **minimum 2 lakh rupees** — NEFT has no minimum.

### The codes on a cheque and beyond
| Code | Size | Job |
|---|---|---|
| **IFSC** (Indian Financial System Code) | **11 characters** | identifies the exact bank branch for NEFT/RTGS/IMPS (e.g. SBIN0001234: 4 letters bank, 0, 6 characters branch) |
| **MICR** (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) | **9 digits** | the cheque number strip at the bottom; speeds cheque clearing |
| **SWIFT** | — | the code system for **international** wire transfers |

### Safety: OTP, PIN, CVV and two factors
- **PIN** = Personal Identification Number (your secret at ATM/UPI); **CVV** = the 3-digit Card Verification Value printed on the card's back; **OTP** = One Time Password, valid for one login/transaction only.
- **Two-factor authentication (2FA)** = password **plus** something else (OTP or fingerprint) — two locks instead of one.
- Real banks **never ask** for PIN, OTP, CVV or passwords by phone, SMS or mail — any such caller is a fraudster. Report cyber-fraud on the national helpline **1930**; IFSC-like codes should never be typed on a link received from a stranger.

### Quick revision
- NEFT = batches, no minimum; **RTGS = real-time, minimum 2 lakh**; IMPS/UPI = instant, 24x7; UPI by NPCI.
- **IFSC = 11 characters** (branch identity); **MICR = 9 digits** (cheque strip); SWIFT = international.
- OTP = one-time password; CVV = 3 digits on card back; 2FA = password + OTP/biometric.
- Banks never ask for OTP/PIN/CVV; cyber-fraud helpline = 1930.

patterns.name: NEFT / RTGS / IMPS / UPI comparison
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which rail has a minimum of 2 lakh', 'which is instant 24x7 by UPI ID', 'full form of NEFT/RTGS/UPI' — the rails' styles mixed in options.
patterns.logic:
1. **NEFT** = batches, half-hourly slots, NO minimum.
2. **RTGS** = real-time gross settlement, **minimum 2,00,000 rupees**.
3. **IMPS** = instant inside banking apps, 24x7.
4. **UPI** = instant app-to-app by UPI ID or QR, built by **NPCI**.
5. The recurring trap: giving NEFT the 2-lakh minimum (it belongs to RTGS).

example.q: A customer must transfer 25,00,000 rupees immediately, transaction by transaction. The suitable system is:
example.solution: **RTGS** — real-time, transaction-wise, built for high-value transfers (minimum 2 lakh).

patterns.name: OTP, PIN, CVV and 2FA safety
patterns.howToSpot: 'Full form of OTP/CVV', 'a caller from the bank asks your OTP — what do you do', or which combination makes an e-transaction two-factor.
patterns.logic:
1. **OTP = One Time Password** — one transaction, one use, short life.
2. **CVV = Card Verification Value** — the 3-digit number on the card's back.
3. **PIN = Personal Identification Number**.
4. **2FA** = password PLUS OTP/biometric — two independent locks.
5. Banks NEVER ask for OTP/PIN/CVV by call, SMS or mail — the asker is a fraudster.

example.q: A caller says he is from your bank and asks for the OTP that just arrived. You should:
example.solution: **Refuse and disconnect — real banks never ask for OTPs**; this is a vishing fraud attempt.

patterns.name: IFSC, MICR and SWIFT codes
patterns.howToSpot: 'IFSC has how many characters', 'which code is used for international transfer', 'the 9-digit code on a cheque is'.
patterns.logic:
1. **IFSC = Indian Financial System Code, 11 characters** — 4 letters (bank) + 0 + 6 (branch); used in NEFT/RTGS/IMPS.
2. **MICR = 9 digits**, the magnetic-ink strip at the cheque's bottom.
3. **SWIFT** = the code system for INTERNATIONAL transfers.

example.q: The number of characters in an IFSC code is:
example.solution: **11** — e.g. SBIN0001234: SBIN (State Bank of India) + 0 + 001234 (branch).

patterns.name: ATM and net-banking basics
patterns.howToSpot: 'ATM stands for', 'which of these can be done at an ATM', 'mobile banking vs net banking' — service identification.
patterns.logic:
1. **ATM = Automated Teller Machine** — cash, balance, mini statement, PIN change, 24x7.
2. Net banking = bank's website; mobile banking = bank's app.
3. ATM transactions need the card + PIN; the PIN is never written on the card.

example.q: The full form of ATM is:
example.solution: **Automated Teller Machine** — the 24x7 machine for cash withdrawal, balance enquiry and mini statements.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Full form of HTTP/HTML/URL/ISP/SMTP/ATM/IFSC/OTP' or a wrongly matched pair where one word of an expansion is changed.
pyqPatterns.approach: Expand letter by letter from family tables: web family (HTTP, HTML, URL, WWW), mail family (SMTP, POP3, IMAP, e-mail @), banking family (NEFT, RTGS, UPI, NPCI, IFSC, MICR, OTP, CVV, PIN, ATM). The planted error is one swapped word, e.g. 'Hyper Transfer Markup Language' for HTML.

example.q: The full form of SMTP is:
example.solution: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol — the sending protocol of e-mail.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which is a browser?' with Google planted among Chrome/Firefox, or 'which is a search engine?' with Chrome planted among Bing/Yahoo.
pyqPatterns.approach: Browsers are programs installed on your device (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari, Opera); search engines are websites reached through them (Google, Bing, Yahoo, DuckDuckGo). The famous trap: Google called a browser, or Chrome called a search engine.

example.q: Which of the following is a web browser?
example.solution: Chrome — the program that shows pages; Google is the search engine inside it.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A mail scenario: who can see whose address, what Reply All reaches, or which field protects a bulk list of receivers.
pyqPatterns.approach: CC is a visible copy (everyone in To/CC sees all those addresses); BCC is blind (To/CC never see the BCC list, and BCC receivers are hidden from each other). Bulk mails to strangers go in BCC; Reply All on a BCC'd mail reaches only the sender.

example.q: A mail to 200 customers uses BCC for all addresses. Reply All by one customer reaches:
example.solution: Only the sender — the BCC list stays hidden.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Protocol used to send e-mail', 'which protocol syncs mail across devices', 'protocol that moves web pages', 'protocol of file transfer' — directions matched.
pyqPatterns.approach: Fix the map: SMTP sends mail; POP3 downloads to one device; IMAP syncs on the server; HTTP/HTTPS move web pages (443 = secure); FTP transfers files; DHCP assigns IPs; DNS resolves names. Sending questions always answer SMTP.

example.q: Which protocol is used to send e-mail from a client to the mail server?
example.solution: SMTP — Simple Mail Transfer Protocol; POP3 and IMAP only receive.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Minimum of 2 lakh belongs to which system?', 'which is instant 24x7', 'full form of NEFT/RTGS/UPI', 'UPI is run by ___' — the rails mixed in options.
pyqPatterns.approach: NEFT = batch transfers, no minimum; RTGS = real-time, transaction-wise, minimum 2,00,000 rupees; IMPS = instant inside banking apps; UPI = instant by UPI ID/QR, built by NPCI. The recurring trap gives NEFT the 2-lakh floor that belongs to RTGS.

example.q: A transfer of 5,00,000 rupees is needed immediately, transaction by transaction. Which system fits?
example.solution: RTGS — real-time gross settlement, designed for high-value transfers (minimum 2 lakh).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A URL is printed and a part is asked: protocol, domain, country code or path; or the full form of URL.
pyqPatterns.approach: Split at slashes: protocol (https://) + domain (www.site.in) + path (/folder/page.html). Country codes: .in India, .uk UK; generic: .com, .org, .gov, .edu. DNS converts the whole domain to an IP address.

example.q: In https://www.mysite.in/exams/ssc.html, 'www.mysite.in' is the:
example.solution: Domain name — https is the protocol; /exams/ssc.html is the path.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which code has 11 characters', 'the 9-digit cheque code', 'the 3-digit number on the card', 'which code for international transfers'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Line them up: IFSC = 11 characters (4 bank letters + 0 + 6 branch) for domestic transfers; MICR = 9 digits on the cheque strip; CVV = 3 digits on the card back; PIN = your secret at machines; OTP = one-time password; SWIFT = international transfers.

example.q: The number of characters in an IFSC code is:
example.solution: 11 — for example SBIN0001234: bank (SBIN) + 0 + branch (001234).

solvedExamples.q: Which of the following is a web browser?
solvedExamples.solution: Microsoft Edge is browser software that displays web pages. Google, Bing and DuckDuckGo are search engines - websites that index the web.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Installed program = browser; website you search inside = engine. Edge/Chrome/Firefox/Safari/Opera are the usual browser options.

solvedExamples.q: An e-mail is sent with the addresses of four colleagues placed in the BCC field. Which statement is correct?
options: All four can see each other's addresses
The To recipients can see the BCC addresses
The four receive copies whose addresses are hidden from other recipients
BCC recipients do not receive attachments
solvedExamples.solution: Blind Carbon Copy hides its recipient list: each BCC recipient gets the full mail (including attachments), but To/CC recipients cannot see who was blind-copied.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 'Blind' = nobody sees the list. The mail itself (with attachments) still arrives.

solvedExamples.q: Which protocol is used to SEND e-mail from a client to a mail server?
solvedExamples.solution: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) handles outgoing mail. POP3 and IMAP fetch incoming mail (POP3 downloads, IMAP syncs), and HTTP serves web pages.
solvedExamples.shortcut: S in SMTP = Send; the receiving protocols are POP3/IMAP.

solvedExamples.q: Match: (a) NEFT (b) RTGS (c) UPI with (i) instant app-based transfer via VPA (ii) batch settlement, no minimum (iii) real-time gross settlement, minimum Rs. 2 lakh
solvedExamples.solution: NEFT settles in half-hourly batches with no minimum amount (a-ii); RTGS settles each transaction individually in real time with a Rs. 2-lakh floor (b-iii); UPI is the instant VPA/QR app rail run by NPCI (c-i).
solvedExamples.shortcut: RTGS grabs the 2-lakh rule; NEFT is the batch rail; UPI is the phone-first instant one.

practice.q: The World Wide Web was invented in 1989 by:
practice.solution: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the WWW at CERN in 1989 and wrote the first browser. Vint Cerf co-designed TCP/IP; Larry Page co-founded Google.
practice.shortcut: Web = Berners-Lee, 1989, CERN. Internet (1970s TCP/IP) = Cerf and Kahn.

practice.q: ARPANET, the precursor of today's Internet, was launched in:
practice.solution: ARPANET went live in 1969 connecting UCLA and Stanford Research Institute, funded by the US Department of Defense.
practice.shortcut: ARPANET 1969 - the 60s birth of the network.

practice.q: The service that translates a domain name like www.ssc.gov.in into an IP address is:
practice.solution: DNS (Domain Name System) resolves human-friendly names to numeric IP addresses. DHCP assigns IP addresses automatically; FTP transfers files; the ISP is your access provider.
practice.shortcut: DNS = the Internet's phonebook: name in, number out.

practice.q: In the URL https://www.ssc.gov.in, the component '.in' is the:
practice.solution: .in is the country-code top-level domain for India. 'https' is the protocol, 'www' the sub-domain/host, 'ssc' the registered domain name.
practice.shortcut: Read right to left: .in = TLD, .gov = second level, ssc = the name.

practice.q: Which of the following is NOT a web browser?
practice.solution: Yahoo is a web portal/search engine, not browser software. Opera, Safari and Firefox are browsers.
practice.shortcut: Scan for the service/brand that you cannot install as a program - that is the odd one.

practice.q: Receiving a file from a web server to your computer is called:
practice.solution: Downloading copies data from the server down to your device; uploading sends it the other way; streaming plays without saving the whole file.
practice.shortcut: Down to you = download; up to the server = upload.

practice.q: The browser shortcut to open a new tab is:
practice.solution: Ctrl+T opens a new tab; Ctrl+N a new window; Ctrl+W closes the current tab; Ctrl+Tab cycles through open tabs.
practice.shortcut: T = Tab, N = window. Ctrl+W wipes the tab.

practice.q: The standard that allows e-mails to carry attachments such as images and documents is:
practice.solution: MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) extends e-mail to carry multimedia, attachments and non-ASCII text. SMTP is the transport protocol for mail.

practice.q: In an e-mail address kiran.ray@nic.in, the part before @ is the:
practice.solution: The format is username@domain: 'kiran.ray' is the user's mailbox name on the domain 'nic.in'.
practice.shortcut: Who@where - the left side is the person.

practice.q: Which e-mail protocol keeps messages on the server so that the same mailbox stays in sync across a phone, tablet and laptop?
practice.solution: IMAP stores mail on the server and synchronises state across devices. POP3 traditionally downloads and removes mail (single-device model), SMTP sends, FTP moves files.

practice.q: The minimum amount that can be transferred through RTGS is:
practice.solution: RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement) is meant for large-value transfers - the floor is Rs. 2 lakh, settled individually and instantly. NEFT carries smaller amounts in batches with no minimum.

practice.q: UPI, the instant real-time payment system, is developed and operated by:
practice.solution: UPI (2016) is built and operated by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), the umbrella organisation for retail payments (it also runs IMPS, RuPay, BHIM). RBI regulates but does not operate UPI.
practice.shortcut: NPCI runs the retail rails: UPI, IMPS, RuPay, AePS. RBI is the regulator.

practice.q: An IFSC code used in electronic fund transfers contains how many characters?
practice.solution: The Indian Financial System Code is 11 characters: 4 letters for the bank, a zero, and 6 characters identifying the branch (e.g. SBIN0007245).

practice.q: Small text files a website stores in your browser to remember sessions and preferences are called:
practice.solution: Cookies hold site-specific data (login sessions, carts, preferences, tracking IDs). They are plain text files - not programs and not viruses.

practice.q: The keyboard shortcut to bookmark (favourite) the current page in all major browsers is:
practice.solution: Ctrl+D adds the current page to bookmarks/favourites. (Ctrl+B is bold in Office; in some browsers it toggles the bookmarks BAR, which is why the safe exam answer for bookmarking a page is Ctrl+D.)

practice.q: The Internet is best described as a —
options: Global network of interconnected computer networks
practice.solution: The Internet is a **network of networks** — no single owner, no single computer.

practice.q: The World Wide Web (WWW) and the Internet are —
options: Two names of the same thing
Different: WWW is a service that runs on the Internet
Different: the Internet runs on the WWW
practice.solution: **Internet = the infrastructure; WWW = hyperlinked pages carried on it** — along with e-mail, FTP and other services.
practice.shortcut: Road system vs traffic on it.

practice.q: ARPANET, the ancestor of the Internet, was launched in —
practice.solution: **ARPANET, 1969** — a US Defence project. 1989 is the WWW's year.

practice.q: Which service does NOT run on the Internet?
practice.solution: E-mail, FTP and VoIP are all Internet services; **punch cards are 1960s input media**, older than the networks.

practice.q: URL stands for —
practice.solution: **URL = Uniform Resource Locator** — the address of a web resource.

practice.q: In the URL https://www.gov.in/schemes/2026.html, the part '/schemes/2026.html' is the —
options: Path to the page on the server
practice.solution: https = protocol, www.gov.in = domain, and everything after is the **path** to the exact file.

practice.q: The '.in' ending of a domain name indicates —
practice.solution: .in is **India's country code**; .com is commercial, .org organisation, .gov government, .edu education.

practice.q: DNS translates —
options: IP addresses into domain names only
practice.solution: **DNS = the Internet's phonebook**: you give a name, it returns the numeric IP the machines use.

practice.q: Which server ASSIGNS an IP address to a device joining a network?
practice.solution: **DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) assigns IPs**; DNS only translates names — the classic swap.

practice.q: The company that provides your Internet connection is called an —
practice.solution: **ISP = Internet Service Provider** (Jio, Airtel, BSNL).

practice.q: HTTP stands for —
practice.solution: **HTTP = HyperText Transfer Protocol** — the rules for moving web pages; HTTPS is its secure version.

practice.q: Which pair is wrongly matched?
practice.solution: HTML = **HyperText Markup Language** — 'Hyper Transfer' is the planted error.

practice.q: Which of the following is a search engine?
practice.solution: **Google indexes and finds pages** — a search engine. Chrome, Firefox and Safari are browsers.

practice.q: Which option lists ONLY web browsers?
practice.solution: All three are browser programs. Option B lists search engines, C lists e-mail services, D lists programming languages.

practice.q: Ctrl+T in a browser opens —
practice.solution: **Ctrl+T = new Tab** (T for tab); Ctrl+N opens a new window.

practice.q: Which shortcut opens the BROWSING HISTORY panel?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+H = History**; Ctrl+J opens the downloads list — the standard trap pair.

practice.q: In Chrome, an incognito window opens with —
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Shift+N** opens Incognito in Chrome; plain Ctrl+N is a normal new window.

practice.q: Match: 1. Ctrl+D 2. Ctrl+F 3. Ctrl+J — a. find on page b. bookmark c. downloads
practice.solution: Ctrl+**D**rops a bookmark, Ctrl+**F**inds on the page, Ctrl+**J** opens downloads.
practice.shortcut: D bookmark, F find, J downloads.

practice.q: Sending a file from your computer to a web server is —
practice.solution: **Upload = you to server; download = server to you.**

practice.q: The browser cache exists mainly to —
options: Speed up revisits by storing copies of pages
practice.solution: **Cache = local copies** of pages and images, so a second visit loads without refetching everything.

practice.q: Which statement about cookies is TRUE?
options: They are viruses that damage files
They are programs that run in background
They are small text files a website stores on your device
They store the pages for offline use
practice.solution: **Cookies = passive text files** (logins, preferences, tracking) — a privacy topic, never a virus.

practice.q: Private (incognito) browsing on a shared computer mainly ensures that —
options: The ISP cannot see your activity
Websites cannot see your visit at all
History and cookies of that session are deleted when the window closes
practice.solution: Incognito forgets **locally** — websites and the ISP still see the traffic.

practice.q: Which action does NOT need an Internet connection?
options: Reading a page saved earlier from the cache/Offline
practice.solution: Only the locally saved copy can be read offline; sending, searching and downloading all need the net.

practice.q: Watching a video as it arrives, without saving the whole file first, is —
practice.solution: **Streaming plays while the data flows in** — the file need not be stored first.

practice.q: In an e-mail, CC stands for —
practice.solution: **CC = Carbon Copy** — a visible duplicate to extra receivers; BCC = Blind Carbon Copy.

practice.q: Receivers in the To and CC fields —
practice.solution: **BCC is blind**: To/CC receivers never see those addresses; each BCC receiver doesn't see the others either.

practice.q: To mail 500 members of an association without exposing their addresses, use —
practice.solution: **BCC hides the list from everyone** — the standard bulk-mail etiquette.

practice.q: Which protocol is used to SEND e-mail?
practice.solution: **SMTP = Simple Mail Transfer Protocol** — it pushes mail out; POP3/IMAP only fetch.

practice.q: Which protocol downloads incoming mail to a single device, usually removing it from the server?
practice.solution: **POP3 = Post Office Protocol** — pick up the mail like a letter-box: one download, one device.
practice.shortcut: POP Picks it off the server.

practice.q: Meera reads her mail on her phone, tablet and laptop, and every device shows the same mailbox. Her account uses —
practice.solution: **IMAP keeps mail on the server and syncs all devices**; POP3 would strand messages on one machine.

practice.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
practice.solution: SMTP sends; POP3 and IMAP receive; web pages travel by HTTP, not POP3.

practice.q: In the e-mail address ramesh.k@gmail.com, the part 'ramesh.k' is the —
practice.solution: **username @ domain** — ramesh.k is the user, gmail.com the mail service.

practice.q: The symbol that separates the username from the domain in an e-mail address is —
practice.solution: **@ means 'at'** — user at this service. It has been the e-mail separator since the 1970s.

practice.q: Which field of an e-mail carries the files clipped to the message?
practice.solution: **Attachments** (paperclip icon) carry files; Subject is the one-line summary; Signature is the sign-off.

practice.q: Unsolicited junk e-mail is called —
practice.solution: **Spam = junk mail**; the filter parks it in the Spam folder.

practice.q: A mail that is written but not yet sent is stored as a —
practice.solution: **Draft** = the waiting room of unsent mail.

practice.q: Reply All on a mail addressed to you and 40 classmates reaches —
options: The sender and everyone on To/CC
practice.solution: **Reply All = sender + To + CC list**; BCC members were never disclosed and stay out.

practice.q: NEFT stands for —
practice.solution: **NEFT = National Electronic Funds Transfer** — batch-wise transfers run by RBI.

practice.q: Which transfer system has a MINIMUM transaction of 2,00,000 rupees?
practice.solution: **RTGS = Real Time Gross Settlement** — built for high-value transfers; minimum 2 lakh. NEFT has no minimum.

practice.q: Which of these moves money INSTANTLY, 24x7, using just a UPI ID or QR code?
practice.solution: **UPI = Unified Payments Interface** — instant app-to-app transfer built by NPCI.

practice.q: Match: 1. NEFT 2. RTGS 3. UPI — a. batch transfers, no minimum b. real-time, minimum 2 lakh c. instant payments by NPCI
practice.solution: NEFT = batches (no minimum), RTGS = real-time with the 2-lakh floor, UPI = NPCI's instant rail.

practice.q: UPI is operated by —
practice.solution: **NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India)** built and runs UPI, IMPS, RuPay and NEFT systems.

practice.q: OTP stands for —
practice.solution: **OTP = One Time Password** — valid for one login or one transaction, for a short time.

practice.q: The 3-digit security number printed on the back of a debit/credit card is the —
practice.solution: **CVV = Card Verification Value** — never share it; it pairs with the card number for online payments.

practice.q: Login by password PLUS an OTP sent to your phone is an example of —
practice.solution: **2FA = two independent proofs** — something you know (password) plus something you receive or are (OTP, fingerprint).

practice.q: A caller claiming to be from your bank asks for the OTP you just received. The correct action is —
options: Share it to verify your account
Refuse and disconnect; banks never ask for OTPs
Send it by SMS for safety
practice.solution: No genuine bank asks for OTP, PIN, CVV or password — this is **vishing** (voice phishing).

practice.q: The secret number typed at the ATM along with the card is the —
practice.solution: **PIN = Personal Identification Number** — card + PIN authorise ATM transactions.

practice.q: An IFSC code contains how many characters?
practice.solution: **IFSC = 11 characters**: 4 letters of the bank + 0 + 6 characters of the branch (SBIN0001234).

practice.q: The 9-digit magnetic-ink code printed at the bottom of a cheque is the —
practice.solution: **MICR = Magnetic Ink Character Recognition** — 9 digits that speed up cheque clearing.

practice.q: For an international wire transfer to your account, the sender needs the —
practice.solution: **SWIFT codes identify banks worldwide** for cross-border transfers; IFSC works only inside India.

practice.q: In the IFSC code SBIN0001234, the first four letters identify the —
practice.solution: SBIN = State Bank of India; the 0 is a separator; **0001234 identifies the branch**.

practice.q: ATM stands for —
practice.solution: **ATM = Automated Teller Machine** — a 'teller' is the person behind the counter; the machine does that job.

practice.q: Which of these can NOT be done at a normal ATM?
options: Opening a new fixed deposit instantly
practice.solution: ATMs handle cash, balance, mini statements and PIN changes; **fixed deposits need the branch, app or net banking**.
practice.shortcut: ATM = cash point, not an FD desk.

practice.q: Banking done through the bank's official app on a phone is called —
practice.solution: **Net banking = website; mobile banking = app** — both run from the same account.
